title: In Afghanistan, Growing Resistance Meets Fears of Pakistani Influence
gist: Five years after the Taliban's return to power, new armed resistance groups such as Sipahiyan-i-Mihan briefly seized a district center in Badakhshan for the first time since 2021, while established fronts led by Ahmad Massoud and General Yasin Zia expand operations amid a deepening humanitarian crisis and growing Afghan suspicion that Pakistan, now in open conflict with the Taliban, is trying to use the resistance as a new instrument of influence.

themes.theme: Emergence of new armed resistance challenging Taliban control

insights.claim: August 15, 2026 marks five years since the Taliban returned to power in Afghanistan, and throughout that period the small armed opposition in Panjshir, Badakhshan, and Baghlan's Andarab district has not managed to successfully contest the Taliban's overall dominance.
insights.speaker: Natiq Malikzada
insights.so_what: Establishes the baseline: five years of largely unsuccessful low-level armed opposition against Taliban rule, against which the new 2026 resistance activity represents a notable escalation.
insights.quote: The small armed opposition in Panjshir, Badakhshan, and Baghlan’s Andarab district has not managed to contest the Taliban’s dominance successfully.
insights.locator: The small armed opposition in Panjshir

insights.claim: A new resistance group called Sipahiyan-i-Mihan ('Soldiers of the Homeland') briefly captured the center of Yaftal-e Payeen district in Badakhshan last month, with fighters entering the district headquarters, disarming Taliban personnel, and raising their flag before withdrawing several hours later.
insights.speaker: Natiq Malikzada
insights.so_what: This is the first documented case since August 2021 of a Taliban district center falling out of government control, a concrete escalation marker for tracking the strength of the emerging Afghan resistance.
insights.quote: Local sources said its fighters entered the district headquarters, disarmed Taliban personnel, and raised their flag.
insights.locator: Last month, a new resistance group

insights.claim: Neither the Taliban nor Sipahiyan-i-Mihan disputes that, for the first time since August 2021, a district center in Afghanistan had fallen out of Taliban control, though they disagree on whether the group's withdrawal was voluntary or a retreat under Taliban reinforcement.
insights.speaker: Natiq Malikzada
insights.so_what: A verified, undisputed loss of territorial control—even temporary—is a hard data point of Taliban vulnerability that both sides confirm, lending it more credibility than contested casualty claims elsewhere in the conflict.
insights.quote: What neither side could deny was that, for the first time since August 2021, a district center had fallen out of Taliban control.

insights.claim: The Taliban sent reinforcements to Yaftal-e Payeen and prepared a larger operation against Sipahiyan-i-Mihan, but as of publication no decisive operation against the group had been publicly reported.
insights.speaker: Natiq Malikzada
insights.so_what: An unresolved Taliban counteroffensive leaves open the possibility of further escalation in Badakhshan, a leading indicator to watch for renewed fighting.
insights.quote: The Taliban later sent reinforcements and prepared a larger operation, but so far, no decisive operation against Sipahiyan-i-Mihan has been publicly reported.

insights.claim: The Republic Front of Afghanistan claimed it targeted a vehicle carrying the Taliban intelligence chief for Kabul's 18th district this week, saying he and his companions were killed; local sources confirmed an explosion occurred but casualties remain unverified.
insights.speaker: Natiq Malikzada
insights.so_what: An attack targeting a Taliban intelligence official inside Kabul itself, rather than in a rural periphery, signals resistance operations are attempting to reach into the Taliban's capital security apparatus.
insights.quote: the Republic Front of Afghanistan said it had targeted a vehicle carrying the Taliban intelligence chief for Kabul’s 18th district and claimed that he and his companions were killed.

insights.claim: The U.S.-based Afghanistan United Front, led by former Afghan army commander General Sami Sadat, announced 'Operation Muharib' and claimed attacks in Kandahar, Helmand, and Badghis provinces.
insights.speaker: Natiq Malikzada
insights.so_what: A U.S.-based, army-commander-led front claiming multi-province operations spanning southern and western Afghanistan indicates the resistance is not confined to the traditional northeastern strongholds like Panjshir and Badakhshan.
insights.quote: The U.S.-based Afghanistan United Front, led by former Afghan army commander General Sami Sadat, also announced “Operation Muharib” and claimed attacks in Kandahar, Helmand, and Badghis.

insights.claim: The established National Resistance Front, led by Ahmad Massoud (son of Ahmad Shah Massoud), and the Afghanistan Freedom Front, led by former army chief General Yasin Zia, have continued and expanded their struggle against the Taliban.
insights.speaker: Natiq Malikzada
insights.so_what: The two most established anti-Taliban fronts expanding operations, alongside multiple new groups, points to a broadening and more organized resistance landscape five years into Taliban rule.
insights.quote: the established National Resistance Front, led by Ahmad Massoud, son of the legendary anti-Taliban commander Ahmad Shah Massoud, and the Afghanistan Freedom Front, led by former army chief General Yasin Zia, have continued and expanded their struggle.

insights.claim: The Afghanistan Freedom Front and the Taliban have clashed for weeks in Badakhshan's Zebak district, with both sides claiming territorial gains and heavy enemy casualties that cannot be independently verified.
insights.speaker: Natiq Malikzada
insights.so_what: Sustained multi-week clashes in a single district indicate a level of resistance capability and Taliban response commitment beyond a single skirmish, marking Zebak as an active flashpoint.
insights.quote: For weeks, the Freedom Front and the Taliban have clashed in Badakhshan’s Zebak district. Both claim gains and heavy casualties, although independent verification remains impossible.

insights.claim: Residents of Zebak confirmed days of fighting, Taliban reinforcements, house-to-house searches, and a frontline visit by the Taliban's chief of army staff, Fasihuddin Fitrat.
insights.speaker: Natiq Malikzada
insights.so_what: A frontline visit by the Taliban's chief of army staff signals the Taliban leadership treats the Zebak clashes as serious enough to warrant top military attention, not a minor local skirmish.
insights.quote: Residents confirmed days of fighting, Taliban reinforcements, house to house searches, and a frontline visit by the Taliban’s chief of army staff, Fasihuddin Fitrat.

themes.theme: Civilian toll of militarization and economic collapse

insights.claim: A resident of Zebak told the author that Taliban fighters have taken over schools and mosques as bases in the district, occupying local civilian infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Natiq Malikzada
insights.so_what: Militarization of civilian infrastructure (schools, mosques) by Taliban forces in contested districts directly harms local service delivery and education access in conflict zones.
insights.quote: Taliban fighters are everywhere, in schools and mosques. They have taken over everything and turned it into their base.

insights.claim: A resident of Zebak said villagers are ordered to provide food for Taliban fighters stationed in their village mosque, despite struggling to feed their own families.
insights.speaker: Natiq Malikzada
insights.so_what: Forced provisioning of Taliban fighters compounds already severe household food insecurity in conflict-affected districts.
insights.quote: We are told to provide food for the Taliban fighters based in our village mosque. But how can we feed them when we can barely feed our own families?
insights.locator: We are told to provide food

insights.claim: A May 2026 U.N. Development Program assessment found that three in four Afghans could not meet their basic needs, while more than 80 percent of households were in debt.
insights.speaker: Natiq Malikzada
insights.so_what: These UNDP figures (75% unable to meet basic needs, 80%+ household debt) quantify a severe humanitarian and economic crisis five years into Taliban rule, critical context for any aid, remittance, or regional stability assessment.
insights.quote: A May 2026 U.N. Development Program assessment found that three in four Afghans could not meet their basic needs, while more than 80 percent of households were in debt.

themes.theme: Pakistan-Taliban rift and fears Pakistan is manipulating the Afghan resistance

insights.claim: Many anti-Taliban Afghans, both inside the country and in the diaspora, have welcomed the new resistance operations, but their hope is mixed with suspicion that Pakistan is trying to use the resistance movements as new instruments of influence after falling into open conflict with its former Taliban partners.
insights.speaker: Natiq Malikzada
insights.so_what: This is the article's central risk framework: Pakistan's rupture with the Taliban creates an incentive for Islamabad to co-opt Afghan resistance groups, a dynamic that could shape which factions gain external funding and legitimacy.
insights.quote: A growing question among some is whether Pakistan, after falling into open conflict with its former Taliban partners, is trying to use the Afghan resistance movements as new instruments of influence.

insights.claim: Pakistan historically supported the Taliban against the former Afghan republic government, and before that against the Mujahideen government in the 1990s, driven by its own security calculations, rivalry with India, and desire for influence in Kabul; the Taliban were the most successful product of that policy.
insights.speaker: Natiq Malikzada
insights.so_what: This historical pattern of Pakistan backing proxy factions in Afghanistan for its own India-rivalry-driven strategic ends is the precedent Afghans now fear could repeat with the new resistance groups.
insights.quote: Pakistan supported the Taliban against the former republic government, and prior to that against the Mujahideen government in the 1990s, always driven by Pakistan’s security calculations, its rivalry with India, and its desire for influence in Kabul.
insights.locator: Mostly, this fear comes from the memory

insights.claim: Pakistan and the Taliban are now fighting over the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), cross-border attacks, and the Taliban's growing engagement with India.
insights.speaker: Natiq Malikzada
insights.so_what: The Taliban's growing engagement with India is cited as one of three specific friction points driving the Pakistan-Taliban rupture, indicating India-Afghanistan ties are now a live irritant in Pakistan-Taliban relations.
insights.quote: Now Pakistan and the Taliban are fighting over the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), cross-border attacks, and the Taliban’s growing engagement with India.

insights.claim: There are credible signs of political outreach by Pakistan to Afghan resistance groups, although there is no public proof that Pakistan is directing or arming any of them.
insights.speaker: Natiq Malikzada
insights.so_what: The distinction between 'credible signs of outreach' and 'no public proof of direction/arming' is an important evidentiary caveat for assessing how far Pakistani involvement in the Afghan resistance actually extends.
insights.quote: There are credible signs of political outreach by Pakistan to the Afghan resistance groups, although no public proof that Pakistan is directing or arming any of them.
insights.locator: There are credible signs of political

insights.claim: In 2025, Islamabad hosted an Afghan dialogue attended by political figures and women activists while the Taliban were absent; organizers called it inclusive and not anti-Taliban, but its location in Islamabad revived Afghan suspicions of Pakistan's intentions.
insights.speaker: Natiq Malikzada
insights.so_what: A Pakistan-hosted opposition dialogue is a concrete, dated (2025) instance of the outreach the article flags as suspicious, useful evidence for tracking Pakistan's engagement with Afghan opposition figures.
insights.quote: In 2025, Islamabad hosted an Afghan dialogue attended by political figures and women activists while the Taliban were absent.

insights.claim: New Lines Magazine reported, citing unnamed sources, that Islamabad had opened channels with Afghan opposition representatives, and rumors suggested certain resistance fronts had opened an office in Pakistan.
insights.speaker: Natiq Malikzada
insights.so_what: Unverified reporting of a resistance-front office in Pakistan, if confirmed, would be a much stronger signal of formal Pakistani-resistance coordination than mere dialogue events.
insights.quote: New Lines Magazine reported, citing unnamed sources, that Islamabad had opened channels with opposition representatives and that rumors suggested certain resistance fronts had opened an office in Pakistan.
insights.locator: Last year, New Lines Magazine reported

insights.claim: Abdullah Azad Khinjani, head of political affairs for the National Resistance Front, told New Lines Magazine that the front remained cautious about Pakistan because the Pakistani establishment has historically sought to 'manage and contain' Afghanistan's opposition.
insights.speaker: Natiq Malikzada
insights.so_what: A named NRF official publicly voicing caution toward Pakistan indicates the resistance's most established faction is deliberately avoiding the appearance of being a Pakistani proxy.
insights.quote: the front remained cautious about Pakistan because the Pakistani establishment historically sought to “manage and contain” Afghanistan’s opposition.
insights.locator: Abdullah Azad Khinjani, head of political

insights.claim: National Resistance Front leader Ahmad Massoud said Afghanistan and Pakistan should build an honest strategic relationship based on mutual respect, but stated he would not accept foreign pressure dictating Afghanistan's decisions; after Pakistan's 2026 attacks he blamed the Taliban's protection of militant groups for regional insecurity while rejecting foreign bombing and insisting Afghanistan's freedom must come through a legitimate, Afghan-led effort.
insights.speaker: Natiq Malikzada
insights.so_what: Massoud's dual position—criticizing the Taliban's militant sheltering while rejecting Pakistani bombing and foreign dictation—is the clearest public template among resistance leaders for balancing anti-Taliban goals with anti-Pakistani-proxy independence.
insights.quote: Afghanistan and Pakistan should build an honest strategic relationship based on mutual respect, but he also made clear that he would not accept foreign pressure dictating Afghanistan’s decisions.

insights.claim: The newer resistance movements discussed in the article have not publicly set out conditions for engagement with Pakistan as clear as those articulated by the National Resistance Front.
insights.speaker: Natiq Malikzada
insights.so_what: The absence of a clear anti-proxy stance from newer groups like Sipahiyan-i-Mihan and the Republic Front leaves them more exposed to suspicion of being usable by Pakistan, a key differentiator among resistance factions worth monitoring.
insights.quote: The newer movements discussed here have not publicly set out comparably clear conditions for any engagement with Pakistan.

insights.claim: An anonymous former Afghan diplomat and resistance supporter said she would not support any resistance group that sides with Pakistan, arguing that Pakistan's bombing campaign in Afghanistan, framed as targeting the Taliban, has instead killed civilians.
insights.speaker: Natiq Malikzada
insights.so_what: This source articulates a hardline red line among segments of the anti-Taliban diaspora: alignment with Pakistan is disqualifying, a sentiment that could limit which resistance factions retain broad Afghan legitimacy.
insights.quote: Any group that sides with Pakistan, I will not support that resistance group. Pakistan is bombing our country, claiming it is killing the Taliban, but the people we see killed are civilians. To side with Pakistan means siding with those killing the people of Afghanistan.

insights.claim: The United Nations said at least 28 civilians were killed in Pakistani operations in Afghanistan in late June 2026, and Amnesty International later called for an investigation into a March strike on a Kabul drug-treatment facility after UNAMA verified at least 269 civilian deaths; Pakistan maintains it targeted militants and military facilities.
insights.speaker: Natiq Malikzada
insights.so_what: UNAMA's verified death toll of at least 269 civilians from a single March strike on a Kabul drug-treatment facility is a hard, sourced casualty figure central to assessing the human cost of the Pakistan-Afghanistan conflict and to any accountability or sanctions discussion.
insights.quote: The United Nations said at least 28 civilians were killed in Pakistani operations in late June, and Amnesty International later called for an investigation into a March strike on a Kabul drug-treatment facility after UNAMA verified at least 269 civilian deaths.
insights.locator: The United Nations said at least

insights.claim: The anonymous resistance supporter said the Taliban are themselves 'a product of Pakistan,' which invested nearly three decades in bringing them to power, and warned that if the current resistance took power and later refused to become Pakistan's puppet, Pakistan would back another group to remove it, continuing a historical cycle.
insights.speaker: Natiq Malikzada
insights.so_what: This source's argument frames the Pakistan-Taliban rupture not as evidence Pakistan and Taliban are now natural enemies, but as one iteration of a recurring Pakistani strategy of installing then discarding Afghan proxies, a lens for skepticism toward any future Pakistan-backed Afghan government.
insights.quote: Pakistan invested nearly three decades in bringing them to where they are. Even if they are enemies now, that does not mean non-Taliban groups should become Pakistan’s allies. If the resistance takes power and later refuses to become Pakistan’s puppet, Pakistan will bring another group to remove it. This cycle has continued until today.

themes.theme: What genuine liberation from Taliban rule would require

insights.claim: On the five-year anniversary of Taliban rule, women and girls in Afghanistan live under a system the author describes as increasingly termed 'gender apartheid,' while millions of Afghans struggle to survive economically.
insights.speaker: Natiq Malikzada
insights.so_what: The 'gender apartheid' framing signals how international human-rights language around Taliban rule has hardened five years in, relevant context for any sanctions, aid conditionality, or diplomatic recognition debates.
insights.quote: with women and girls living under a system increasingly described as gender apartheid and millions struggling to survive, the desire for change is understandable and urgent.

insights.claim: The author argues that any alternative to Taliban rule must be built inside Afghanistan, answerable to its own people, inclusive of women and communities, and independent enough to cooperate with neighbors without becoming their instrument of influence, or else it risks repeating history's cycle of proxy rule.
insights.speaker: Natiq Malikzada
insights.so_what: This is the article's normative bottom line: the viability and legitimacy of any post-Taliban resistance-led government hinges on demonstrable independence from foreign patrons like Pakistan, a criterion for assessing which resistance factions merit international support.
insights.quote: the alternative Afghans are searching for must be built inside Afghanistan, answerable to its people, inclusive of its women and communities, and independent enough to cooperate with neighbors without becoming their instrument of influence.
